one_liner: Small C WebAssembly interpreter (miniwasm) plus wat/wasm tools; first-party charts show it 1.06-2.6x faster than wasm3 in 2023.
what_it_does: Web49 is a C toolkit holding miniwasm (a WASI-capable command-line wasm interpreter that also runs .wat and .wast files) and small rewrites of wat2wasm, wasm2wat and wasm2wasm (an LEB128-shrinking re-emitter). Use it as a command (miniwasm file.wasm args) or embed it through src/interp/interp.h (web49_interp_module, web49_interp_add_import_func, web49_interp_block_run). It is not API-compatible with wasm3's m3_* embedding API.
how_it_is_fast: Each function is translated lazily, on first call, from stack bytecode into a register-style threaded code: operands are local-slot indices or inline constants, so most pushes and pops disappear. Before that, an expression-tree pass (src/opt/tree.c) and a tee-to-set pass (src/opt/tee.c) rebuild operand trees, and compares that feed a branch are fused into compare-and-branch instructions (IF_I32_EQ, IF_I32_LT_S and so on). At the benchmarked commit, dispatch was computed-goto direct threading (goto *head++->opcode). The record's claim that it uses basic-block versioning from MiniVM does not show up in the interpreter source.
when_to_use: Running trusted, compute-bound wasm32 modules (recursion, integer and float loops such as fib, fannkuch, binary-trees) where a small C interpreter with no JIT is required and the 2023 numbers against wasm3 are enough evidence.
Projects that want a wasm interpreter and a wat2wasm/wasm2wat toolchain in one small MIT-licensed C codebase that builds with a plain makefile and gcc, clang or tcc.
Experiments or teaching on interpreter design (lazy stack-to-register translation, superinstructions, threaded dispatch), where readable C source matters more than spec conformance.
Shrinking LLVM-emitted .wasm files with wasm2wasm, which re-encodes over-long LEB128 numbers (0-4 bytes saved per 32-bit number, per the README).
when_not_to_use: Untrusted or sandboxed code: at HEAD the bounds check computes addr + size in 32-bit arithmetic, so accesses within 7 bytes of 4 GiB pass the check and touch host memory past the linear-memory buffer; random_get writes through &memory[ptr] with no check at all, and base + offset effective addresses wrap instead of trapping in both versions checked (70dd3e6 and HEAD).

Anything that needs a conformant engine: the committed results.txt passes 39 of the 147 spec .wast files (39 of 90 non-SIMD, 0 of 57 SIMD), well below the README's '~75%'; issue #4 (jedisct1, open since 2023-01-09) reports libsodium's scalarmult crashing and xchacha20 giving wrong results.

Programs that write to stdout: the current WASI fd_write ignores the fd and prints every iovec to stderr with an extra newline (the 2023 version wrote correctly); only a handful of WASI calls are implemented.

Workloads that trap often or run many short-lived modules where trap cost matters: the trap chart is about 5x slower than wasm3 (about 0.027 s vs 0.0055 s). At HEAD every trap is a __builtin_trap() process crash, not a recoverable error.
Production or long-term use: development stopped in May 2023 apart from one build-system refactor commit (2025-11-06); there is one release (v0.0.1), the API is unversioned and 8 issues are open.

integration.form: source-drop (makefile builds the miniwasm, wat2wasm, wasm2wat, wasm2wasm and wat2wat binaries; no installed library or package)
integration.dependencies: none beyond libc and libm (getentropy for WASI random_get); bench.py needs Python 3 with matplotlib, emcc and the engines it compares
integration.min_toolchain: GNU C extensions (statement expressions, __builtin_trap, and computed goto when WEB49_USE_SWITCH is 0); gcc, clang or tcc per the README; MSVC needs the NEXT/LABEL macros rewritten; compiler versions not documented
integration.platforms: Portable C; CI built Linux, macOS and Windows (gcc) release binaries in 2023; the published benchmarks ran on Apple M1 (aarch64)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the interpreter passes a web49_interp_t by value and keeps a function-static dispatch table, and no threads proposal or shared memory is supported
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: as a command it runs the same WASI .wasm files as the wasm3 CLI (for the WASI calls it implements), but the embedding API differs from wasm3's

gotchas: Harness flaws: bench.py times one run per test (ten for trap) with time.time() around subprocess.call, ignores both engines' exit codes and sends stdout to DEVNULL, so a crashed or wrong run would still be charted. The 'mandelbrot-simd' test uses GCC vector extensions, but bench.py passed no -msimd128 to emcc at the chart commit, so neither engine executed wasm SIMD. 'fib_i32' computes with uint64_t (i64 ops), which is why its chart matches fib_i64.

The charts (commit 70dd3e6, 2023-01-09) are not reproducible from HEAD: the 2025 makefile typo 'CLAGS_opt = -O3' means the README's 'make CC=gcc' builds miniwasm without any -O flag (link-only -flto); src/config.h now defaults to WEB49_USE_SWITCH 1 (switch dispatch rather than the benchmarked computed goto); and bench.py now also runs wasmer and wasmtime and leaves coremark out.

Memory-safety bugs at HEAD (src/interp/interp.h web49_interp_addr, src/wasi/wasi.c random_get) let a module read or write host memory near linear-memory base + 4 GiB. At 70dd3e6 the size check was done in 64-bit arithmetic, but the uint32 effective-address wrap was already there.

Unpublished charts in res/ (nop, fib_f32, fib_f64, fib_i64) are also favorable: fib_f32/fib_f64 about 4.85 s vs 1.85 s, fib_i64 about 3.1 s vs 1.2 s, nop about 5 ms vs 1.6 ms (read by eye). So the README selection is not cherry-picked against miniwasm, but none of these were rerun on current code.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose wasm3 (the incumbent) or WAMR's fast interpreter whenever you need spec conformance, sandboxing or an embedding API. UWVM2 has much broader evidence of beating wasm3 (geomean 0.5957 over 383 modules). Web49 only makes sense for trusted modules where you want a very small C interpreter and wat/wasm tooling in one codebase and can live with its gaps.
verified_claims_summary: On a 2020 MacBook Air (M1, 8 GiB), single wall-clock runs of emcc -O2 C benchmarks put miniwasm ahead of wasm3 (wasm3 version and build unstated) by about 2.6x on fib(40), 1.5x on binary-trees 16, 1.4x on fannkuch-redux 10, 1.25x on nbody and 1.06-1.2x on mandelbrot and coremark. A trap was about 5x slower. All figures are read by eye from first-party PNG charts made at commit 70dd3e6 (January 2023), with no output or exit-code checks.
status_note: Effectively dormant since May 2023 (one build-refactor commit on 2025-11-06 that introduced the -O typo); MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but its HEAD has memory-safety and WASI-output bugs, so a vendored copy should start from a reviewed commit and be limited to trusted code.
